answer.evidence: No first-layer unit has a tight, high-magnitude, same-sign block of weights in a corner, edge or other off-nodule spot, which is the signature an artificial marker or patch would usually leave. Most of the units with visible learned structure concentrate it in the central region, roughly rows 4-19 and cols 4-21, where the nodule sits. Units 3, 8, 24, 27 and 28 have mostly strong positive weights (up to about 95-99) there; unit 21 does too, though its positive region is broader. Units 5 and 29 have negative centres, and units 2 and 18 combine a negative centre with positive periphery, which reads as a contrast between the nodule and its surroundings. A few units lean mildly positive along the right edge: unit 16 at cols 20-23, rows 0-19, mean weight about +27, plus units 2, 14, 20 and 30. The top rows 0-3 show a similar mild positive lean across many units. These edge and top-row patterns are much weaker than the central structure. Rough path products through layers 2 and 3 also give them inconsistent signs: units 20 and 30 push toward malignant, while units 2, 14, 16, 19 and 25 push toward benign. So they look like diffuse context features (surrounding tissue or chest-wall brightness) rather than a consistent spurious cue. This check was done by hand and ignores the second-layer ReLUs, so a subtle shortcut cannot be ruled out.
answer.main_feature: The model mainly responds to bright, dense tissue in the central region where the nodule lies, using broad centre-positive detectors (units 3, 8, 24, 27, 28) and centre-versus-surround contrast units (2, 5, 18, 29). Larger, denser central opacities push the output toward malignant.
